**The meaning of the verse**
﴿وَقَضَىٰ رَبُّكَ أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ وَبِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا ۚ إِمَّا يَبْلُغَنَّ عِندَكَ الْكِبَرَ أَحَدُهُمَا أَوْ كِلَاهُمَا فَلَا تَقُل لَّهُمَا أُفٍّ وَلَا تَنْهَرْهُمَا وَقُل لَّهُمَا قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا﴾

Your Lord, O man, has commanded, made binding and obligatory that He alone, glorified and exalted is He, be singled out for worship, and He has commanded kindness to father and mother, especially in old age if they are in your care. So do not become impatient or find burdensome anything you see from one or both of them, and do not let them hear a bad word, not even "uff," which is the very least of bad words, and let no ugly deed come from you towards them. Rather, be gentle with them, and always speak to them with soft, kind words.

📖 At-Tafsir Al-Muyassar — King Fahd Complex.

**Talk with your child**
1. What did Ruqayya say every time her mother called her? And what word did she say when she finally got up?
2. Why was her mother's look heavier on Ruqayya than any scolding? And what did she remember in the night, and hear before Fajr?
3. What did Ruqayya do to put things right? And is it enough to do what our parents ask while saying "uff"? (No; the verse forbids "uff" itself, so dutifulness is in the word and the tone of voice just as it is in the deed.)

**This week's exercise**
Agree with your child on a kind sentence to say instead of "uff" when they are called while busy, such as: "Coming, I'll just finish this and be right there," and then they really do come. At the end of each day, ask them: How many times did you say it today?
